Australian Electrical Equipment Industry Faces Credit Freeze, Major Disruptions Across Firms

The Australian electrical equipment industry is confronting a deepening financial crisis this week as a sudden credit freeze has gripped the sector, halting access to working capital for several major companies and hundreds of mid-sized firms. Industry analysts point to tightening lending standards by domestic banks and a sharp decline in available trade finance, leaving many businesses unable to secure the funding required for ongoing operations and payroll.

Rexel Group Australia Pty Ltd, a leading distributor in the industry, confirmed in a statement that it is actively reviewing its liquidity position amid what it called “extraordinary market conditions.” The company has implemented immediate cost-control measures, including a hiring freeze and the suspension of non-essential capital expenditure. “We are working closely with our banking partners to secure lines of credit and ensure supply continuity to our customers,” a spokesperson for Rexel Group Australia Pty Ltd said. “Our priority is to support our teams and maintain service wherever possible.”

Industry-wide, the credit freeze has forced a wave of production slowdowns and temporary closures at manufacturing and distribution sites, particularly in New South Wales and Victoria. According to the Electrical Equipment Manufacturers Association of Australia, at least 15% of the sector’s workforce—estimated at over 2,000 positions—have been furloughed or placed on reduced hours in the past fortnight. “This is an unprecedented situation for the industry,” said association president Angela Kerr. “Many firms are struggling to meet payroll obligations and keep essential operations running.”

Several mid-sized companies, such as Austrogen Controls and PowerSwitch Solutions, have reported delays in fulfilling existing orders due to a lack of working capital and the inability to finance inventory purchases. Workers at affected sites have expressed concern about job security, with some unions calling for urgent government intervention to stabilize the sector. “Our members are worried about their futures and whether their jobs will exist next month,” said Michael Tran, state secretary of the Electrical Trades Union.

The outlook remains uncertain as industry participants await signs of relief from lenders or potential policy responses. For now, the credit freeze continues to create widespread disruption throughout Australia’s electrical equipment industry, with firms, sites, and workers all feeling the impact.
